title: Tenant Isolation
explain: For a multi-tenant system there are two ways to scale: pool everyone in one shared fleet, or give each tenant or group of tenants its own instances and skip cross-tenant horizontal scaling. Isolation trades utilization and operations for simplicity and blast-radius control, and in practice I run a hybrid: pool the small tenants, silo the large or regulated ones.
model:
Split by tenant first, scale within a tenant only if you must. (Chinese mnemonic: 多 instance 直接分 tenant, 不搞横向扩展了.)

```
Pooled:   [ shared fleet, every request carries tenant_id ] <- scale horizontally
Siloed:   [ instance for A ] [ instance for B ] [ instance for C+D ]
Hybrid:   pooled fleet for the long tail  +  silos for big or regulated tenants
```

Isolation ladder, weakest to strongest: a `tenant_id` column (needs row-level security and quotas), a schema, a database, a cluster, an account.

| | Pooled | Siloed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Utilization | High | Idle instances still cost |
| Operations | One thing to run | N things to deploy, monitor, migrate |
| Noisy neighbour / blast radius | Shared | Contained |
| Per-tenant needs (residency, keys, versions) | Hard | Natural |
| One huge tenant | Scales horizontally | Capped by one instance |

Make tenants movable ([rebalance](#/sd/f/rebalance)) so a growing tenant can graduate from pool to silo. [Compartments](#/sd/f/compartment) draw the logical boundary; [cells](#/sd/f/cell) are the extreme version.

details.q: A SaaS gives each of its 200 customers a dedicated instance and calls scaling solved. One customer reaches 60 percent of traffic. What is the limit?
details.a: That customer is still capped by one instance, so it needs partitioning or horizontal scaling inside its own silo. Isolation moves the scaling problem, it does not remove it.

details.q: 50,000 free-tier tenants plus a few enterprise customers with data-residency contracts. What design?
details.a: Pooled shared fleet for the free tier, dedicated silos for the contract customers. Siloing the long tail wastes money; pooling the regulated customers fails their contracts.

details.q: What does siloing cost in dollars at small-tenant scale?
details.a: If a silo costs $20 per month idle, 5,000 free tenants cost $100,000 per month before any real work. That is the utilization argument for pooling small tenants.

details.q: In a pooled database, what actually protects tenants from a noisy neighbour?
details.a: Per-tenant rate limits and quotas, and caps on connections and query concurrency. A `tenant_id` filter or index does not isolate load; it only separates data.

details.q: How do you move a large tenant from the pool to a silo without downtime?
details.a: Provision the silo, copy the tenant's existing data while the pool keeps serving, stream changes until the silo catches up, switch routing for that tenant, then delete its data from the pool after verification. It is a [backfill](#/sd/f/backfill) plus a cutover.

details.q: When would you refuse to silo?
details.a: Thousands of tiny tenants with no special requirements: the operations burden and idle cost outweigh the isolation benefit. Pool them and rely on quotas.

prompts.q: Compare pooled and siloed multi-tenancy and say how you would combine them.
points: Pooled: shared horizontally scaled fleet, efficient, noisy neighbours
Siloed: dedicated instances, strong isolation, per-tenant needs easy
Silo costs: idle utilization, more operations, one tenant capped by its silo
Hybrid: pool small, silo large or regulated
Keep tenant migration between them routine

prompts.q: Explain the isolation ladder and what each level gives.
points: tenant_id column with row-level security is weakest
Schema, database, cluster, account get stronger
Stronger means more cost and operations
Choose the level per tenant need

prompts.q: Protect a pooled system from a noisy tenant.
points: Caps on connections and query concurrency
Move the heavy tenant to a silo if limits are not enough
